importance_ranking.reason: Visual sub-type variation is extreme — A-frame, round log, D-log, modern timber frame, and resort cottage cluster are visually distinct products. Buyers have a specific aesthetic vision; image is the primary product-type identifier and the first shortlisting gate.

Wood type, log profile, floor area, and treatment are non-interchangeable project requirements. A buyer specifying cedar cannot substitute pine; a resort developer needing 600 sq ft cottages cannot use a 200 sq ft cabin spec. Specs are the primary technical shortlisting gate after visual match.

importance_ranking.brand_important_reason: No dominant brand with buyer recall exists in the Indian log home market; it is fragmented across regional manufacturers and buyers search by spec, portfolio, and geography rather than brand name.
importance_ranking.reason: High-value custom build over 45–90 days — buyers evaluate manufacturer track record, completed project portfolio, installation geography, and post-sale support before committing. Seller identity is a significant trust signal for a project of this scale.

Per-sq-ft rate varies substantially with wood species, floor area, and construction method. Indian buyers are price-sensitive but listed price is a budget entry point — final price is always negotiated for a custom project. Price is compared only after spec and visual equivalence is confirmed.

importance_ranking.unit_note: Some sellers quote per unit or per project lump sum for kit-form cabins and resort cottage clusters — creates real price comparison confusion. Per sq ft must be shown alongside price to enable meaningful comparison.
importance_ranking.reason: Price cannot be compared across sellers without knowing the unit. Per sq ft vs per unit vs per project is a genuine market ambiguity in this category; unit display is essential for buyer price interpretation.

top_configurator_specs.reason: Non-interchangeable material class — teak vs engineered wood vs pine represents a 3–5x price difference and buyers cannot substitute one species for another based on project requirements.
Defines project scale directly — the largest single driver of total project cost, and a 300 sq ft cabin is not substitutable for a 1000 sq ft villa regardless of other specs.

missing_important_specs.why_important: Structural and thermal performance spec cited by Indian manufacturers (90–120 mm range) — resort and hill-station buyers specify this for insulation adequacy and structural integrity, and it drives material cost directly.
Hill-station and cold-climate buyers require PUF or equivalent insulation panels for thermal performance — absence of this spec prevents buyers from confirming suitability for their climate zone.

Prefabricated modular vs site-built vs kit-form determines build timeline (45–90 days for prefab vs months for site-built) and total project cost — a primary decision variable for resort developers on tight opening schedules.

top_rfq_specs.reason: BHK configuration immediately communicates project scale and complexity to sellers — a 1 BHK studio vs 3 BHK villa defines feasibility, floor area range, and price tier before any other spec is needed.
Wood species is non-interchangeable and defines the material tier — sellers need this to confirm supply capability and provide an accurate per-sq-ft rate rather than a wide indicative range.

missing_important_specs.why_important: Sellers need explicit floor area to confirm project feasibility and provide an accurate quote — BHK configuration is a partial proxy but does not capture the actual built-up area the buyer requires.

buyer_spec_audit.image_upload_reason: Log home buyers frequently have a specific design reference — a cabin style, roof form, facade aesthetic, or competitor resort cottage they want to replicate — that cannot be captured in spec dropdowns. An uploaded reference image allows sellers to assess design complexity, confirm they can replicate the style, and provide a more accurate initial quote rather than a wide indicative range.
